video_title: BlackRock Confirmed Bitcoin Is Here To Stay
gist: Jay Jacobs, BlackRock's US head of equity ETFs, argues the Bitcoin ETP (IBIT) changed Bitcoin's investor mix and volatility without changing its underlying diversifying role, and that in-kind creation is now driven less by custody fears than by the desire to borrow against and write options on Bitcoin inside a wrapper. He also lays out BlackRock's view that AI has become a macro factor, that AI demand is compounding exponentially while copper, indium and fab supply lag 4-8 years, and that the best AI opportunities may now sit outside the tech sector in utilities, materials and data-center real estate.

insights.claim: BlackRock's Jay Jacobs argues the single biggest measurable impact of spot Bitcoin ETPs was removing the operational barrier of digital asset exchange onboarding, turning Bitcoin exposure into a brokerage-account click for individuals, RIAs and institutions alike.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Access, not price forecasting, was the marginal driver of the last flow cycle - watch adviser-platform approvals as the leading indicator of the next tranche of demand rather than retail sentiment.
insights.quote: once the Bitcoin ETPs like IBIT came out, it just made it as easy to access as clicking a button on a brokerage account just like you buy the S&P 500 or buy an individual stock

insights.claim: Before IBIT existed, advisers and institutions could rationally deprioritize Bitcoin entirely because they had no way to act on a view; once an approved vehicle existed, Bitcoin became a mandatory agenda item in asset-allocation committees.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Product availability forces institutional due diligence, which means allocation decisions are still working through committees - a structural, slow-moving bid rather than a one-time flow event.
insights.quote: Once exposure to Bitcoin became available to them with IBIT, it had to be a part of the conversation of how do they think about this asset class?

insights.claim: BlackRock's digital asset product strategy is deliberately narrow-and-deep rather than broad-and-many, anchored on the claim that Bitcoin and Ethereum alone represent roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of total digital asset market cap.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Do not expect the largest issuer to chase altcoin ETPs; the competitive opening for smaller issuers is in long-tail coins, while BlackRock competes on liquidity and structure variants of BTC and ETH.
insights.quote: remember Bitcoin and Ethereum make up anywhere between 2/3 and 3/4 of the whole digital asset market cap

insights.claim: BlackRock built variants rather than new coins - a staked Ethereum ETP (ETHB) alongside an unstaked version, and a Bitcoin premium income product overwriting roughly 30% of the exposure with covered calls - explicitly because clients said a zero-yielding asset is hard to slot into cash-flow-driven portfolios.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Yield-wrapping is how crypto gets into income mandates; expect further option-overlay and staking variants to be the growth vector rather than new underlying assets.
insights.quote: the fact that it's a zero coupon, zero yielding asset um makes it sometimes hard to fit in a portfolio that can be very kind of cash flow based

insights.claim: Bitcoin's realized volatility has compressed from roughly 80 to roughly 35-40, a shift the host attributes variously to Wall Street participation, the ETFs themselves, or the leverage and options layered on top.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: A halving of vol changes position sizing math for risk-parity and vol-targeting allocators, mechanically allowing larger Bitcoin weights at the same risk budget.
insights.quote: It was, you know, 80ish vault asset. Now it's like a 3540 vault asset.

insights.claim: Jacobs attributes Bitcoin's volatility compression to two mechanisms - the ETP options market giving complex trades a venue to clear, and a larger base of researched, long-term holders acting as counterbalance to short-term traders - rather than to any single cause.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: If vol compression is structural (market depth) rather than cyclical, it should persist through drawdowns - a testable assumption that breaks loudly if it fails in the next stress event.

insights.claim: The host puts to Jacobs that Bitcoin has undergone a 'silent IPO' - a transfer of ownership from early asymmetric-return holders to a new rate-sensitive, higher-correlation investor base - a framing borrowed from Jordi Visser.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: If the marginal Bitcoin holder now trades off Fed and inflation prints, macro data becomes a higher-frequency driver of BTC than crypto-native catalysts.
insights.quote: It does feel like Bitcoin now is much more interest rate sensitive. It trades with higher correlations to certain assets.

insights.claim: BlackRock concedes the ownership mix and volatility have changed but explicitly rejects the idea that Bitcoin's fundamental characteristics have shifted, maintaining it remains a decentralized global monetary alternative that should outperform precisely when institutional, geopolitical and fiat-debasement fears hurt stocks and bonds.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The largest issuer is still selling Bitcoin as a crisis diversifier, not a risk asset - a positioning that will be tested the next time BTC sells off alongside equities.
insights.quote: So that fundamental diversifying nature of Bitcoin we believe still very much holds uh even as the investor base has maybe shifted over the last few years.

insights.claim: Jacobs says he initially expected in-kind creation demand to come from self-custody holders wanting institutional custody, but the dominant actual driver turned out to be financialization - borrowing against Bitcoin and overlaying option strategies once it sits inside a wrapper.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The wrapper's value is collateral utility, not safety - suggesting demand for Bitcoin-backed lending and structured products grows faster than pure custody migration.
insights.quote: a bigger piece of it is actually the ability to kind of financialize Bitcoin. Uh borrow against it is a huge use case

insights.claim: The minimum size for an in-kind IBIT transaction has fallen to roughly $1.5 million from a substantially higher prior threshold, widening the pool of Bitcoin holders who can swap coins for ETF shares.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A lower in-kind minimum converts long-held coins into ETF shares without a taxable sale - a quiet supply channel from cold storage into regulated wrappers worth monitoring in creation data.
insights.quote: right now it's sort of at the $1.5 million level for an inkind transaction. Previously it was much higher than that.

insights.claim: Once Bitcoin sits inside the ETF wrapper, holders can run protective option strategies, income overlays, or exchange-replication trades that reduce Bitcoin risk and swap into something like S&P 500 exposure - options unavailable to raw coin holders.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Concentrated crypto wealth now has tax-aware diversification routes, which could mute the forced-selling dynamic that historically accompanied large holders de-risking.

insights.claim: BlackRock deliberately keeps itself out of both market making and the in-kind exchange mechanism, outsourcing those to third parties despite having the scale to do them, treating that restraint as a core competency.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The largest issuer is not vertically integrating into trading, which preserves the independent market-maker and APs ecosystem that competitors and liquidity providers depend on.
insights.quote: We're not a market maker. We're not setting out markets on an individual ETF, but we have relationships with market makers.

insights.claim: BlackRock has for several months been telling clients that AI adoption now sits alongside GDP growth and interest rates as a primary macro input to market direction, not as a sector theme.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: If the largest asset manager models AI adoption as a macro variable, AI capex guidance becomes a market-wide risk factor - hedging it requires index-level, not sector-level, positioning.
insights.quote: AI has effectively become a macro factor

insights.claim: Jacobs frames US market price levels as directly levered to the pace of AI, arguing an AI slowdown would be felt across markets and an acceleration would lift them.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Concentration risk is now systemic rather than idiosyncratic - a diversified US equity portfolio carries implicit AI beta whether or not it holds AI names.
insights.quote: if AI slows down the markets will feel it if AI accelerates the markets will enjoy it like it is that important to especially the US markets

insights.claim: BlackRock argues investors misclassify AI as a tech theme when it is simultaneously a healthcare, legal and consumer theme, meaning a healthcare fund allocation does not actually reduce AI exposure.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Investors who think they are diversified away from AI by rotating into defensive sectors may be double-counting the same factor - a reason to measure AI exposure at the factor level.
insights.quote: Too many people, I think, still view AI as a tech theme.

insights.claim: BlackRock's AI value chain framework spans power companies, data-center real estate, chip manufacturers, data owners, LLM developers, adopting applications and enabling platforms - now dozens of companies globally across many sectors.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Use the value-chain map to find where the marginal dollar of AI capex lands next, rather than repeatedly buying the same US large-cap names.

insights.claim: BlackRock believes some of the best AI opportunities currently sit outside technology, in the physically constrained parts of the chain - materials, utilities and real estate - because software scales at no incremental cost while compute has a large physical footprint.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: This is an explicit steer away from crowded semis-and-hyperscaler exposure toward power, mining and data-center REIT plays on the same AI dollar.
insights.quote: And in fact some of the best opportunities we think sort of sit outside of tech right now.

insights.claim: Jacobs identifies the core mismatch in AI as exponential demand growth - with LLMs writing their own improvement code around the clock and companies raising token budgets in days or weeks - against a supply side measured in years.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Persistent supply shortfall means pricing power accrues to physical bottleneck owners rather than model developers - a multi-year relative-value case for hard-asset AI inputs.
insights.quote: So the models are getting much better very quickly. The demand is growing at an exponential rate, but the supply side is lagging by years.

insights.claim: New copper supply needed for data centers and US grid rebuild takes an estimated 4 to 8 years to bring a mine online, making copper a structural choke point on AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Copper's lead time cannot compress on demand signals, so shortages resolve through price rather than volume - a direct case for copper miner exposure as an AI derivative.
insights.quote: you could be looking at 4 to 8 years until that copper mine comes online

insights.claim: If photonics and lasers displace copper for in-data-center data transmission, the binding input becomes indium, which is only a small byproduct of zinc mining and processing - creating an even longer and more obscure supply chain.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A non-obvious second-order trade: substituting away from copper does not remove the materials bottleneck, it moves it to a byproduct metal with even less elastic supply.

insights.claim: Even with aggressive acceleration, new semiconductor fabs take about four years to bring online in the United States, capping how fast GPU supply can respond to demand.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: GPU scarcity is a multi-year condition regardless of policy support, sustaining margins for incumbent chip supply and its memory and packaging adjacencies.
insights.quote: the fabs take about four years to bring online even in the United States

insights.claim: BlackRock screens product innovation on three pillars - whether it solves a client need or defines an otherwise inaccessible slice of a value chain, whether it carries positive expected return and portfolio utility, and whether a quality ETF can actually be built around it.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: This is the filter that determines which AI sub-themes get an institutional-scale vehicle, and therefore which get sustained flows.

insights.claim: Jacobs argues that drilling into AI sub-sub-themes with only a couple of eligible names stops resembling an ETF and becomes largely undoable in the structure, setting a hard floor on how narrow thematic products can go.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Ultra-narrow single-component ETFs face structural limits, so the proliferation of hyper-specific vehicles from smaller issuers carries concentration and liquidity risk the wrapper was not built for.
insights.quote: when you get really narrow into the sub sub themes of artificial intelligence and there's only a couple of names, it doesn't really resemble an ETF anymore

insights.claim: BlackRock's answer to unpredictable rotation within AI is a barbell of one actively managed all-in-one AI ETF (BAI) plus index-based sleeves for specific bottlenecks - power (PWR), digital infrastructure and data-center real estate (IDGT), and copper mining (ICOP).
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The sleeve lineup is a public map of where BlackRock thinks AI bottlenecks rotate next - power, digital real estate, copper - and gives a ready-made expression for each.

insights.claim: BAI is run by fundamental equities manager Tony Kim as an active stock-picking portfolio that rotates across the AI value chain, in contrast to rules-based index sleeves like the power ETF which evolve only by index methodology.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The active-versus-index distinction matters for who bears the rotation timing risk - outsource it to BAI, or take bottleneck-specific index risk yourself.

insights.claim: BAI was intentionally designed and distributed as a funding swap out of an investor's existing tech sector allocation, keeping sector and geography exposure roughly neutral while concentrating in the better parts of technology.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Answering 'what do I sell' is the actual distribution unlock for thematic products - a template for judging which new theme funds will gather assets.
insights.quote: BAI is designed to be you're selling your tech sector and you're allocating to BAI

insights.claim: BlackRock runs over 480 ETFs in the US and says it has declined roughly as many or more product concepts, framing the refusal rate as the discipline behind the lineup.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Scale plus a stated veto rate means BlackRock will lag on novelty launches - the first-mover window in niche themes stays open for smaller issuers.
insights.quote: we still have over 480 ETFs in the US

themes.theme: ETF structure, tax and liquidity mechanics

insights.claim: There are now more ETFs listed in the US than stocks, this is tracking as a record year for launches, and active ETFs now outnumber index-based ETFs - a breadth problem Jacobs names as a genuine risk to investor decision quality.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Selection risk has migrated from picking stocks to picking wrappers - identically named AI or power ETFs can hold very different portfolios under the hood.
insights.quote: there's more ETFs than there are stocks listed in the United States

insights.claim: BlackRock structured its Bitcoin premium income product as a '33 Act vehicle - the same structure used for Bitcoin and gold ETFs - rather than the '40 Act structure used by almost all other ETFs, accepting K-1 complexity in exchange for better after-tax outcomes.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Structure choice, not the ticker or fee, can drive after-tax return in crypto-income products - a diligence point when comparing superficially identical Bitcoin covered-call funds.

insights.claim: Jacobs pushes back on the blanket claim that ETFs are inherently the most tax-efficient vehicle, noting that funds holding options, futures or bonds behave very differently from equity ETFs as the wrapper is pushed into more strategies.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The tax-efficiency assumption breaks down exactly in the derivative-heavy products currently growing fastest - check the underlying instruments before assuming ETF tax treatment.
insights.quote: it's not as simple as saying ETFs are the most tax efficient vehicle

insights.claim: BlackRock built systematic rotation ETFs - ingesting hundreds of global data points for buy and sell signals across themes, factors and countries - specifically because clients find selling harder than buying and because DIY rotation triggers capital gains that the ETF wrapper can defer.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Tax-deferred thematic rotation inside a wrapper is a real structural edge over doing the same trades in a taxable account - relevant to any high-turnover theme strategy.

insights.claim: Two ETFs with identical mandates can deliver very different liquidity in stressed markets depending on the breadth and quality of the issuer's market-maker relationships, which BlackRock designs for at product construction.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: In a liquidity event, spread and NAV tracking will diverge sharply between same-name ETFs - a reason to prefer vehicles with deep AP support even at a higher fee.
insights.quote: I'm going to bet the ETF that has a more robust market making community around it and better relationships is probably going to have a better liquidity experience

insights.claim: Jacobs says mutual funds remain the predominant structure in retirement accounts because tax efficiency, liquidity and daily transparency matter little to biweekly long-only contributors, so the ETF's default status applies mainly to liquid taxable markets.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The mutual fund to ETF migration is not uniform - retirement assets are a defended pool, which bounds the addressable conversion opportunity for ETF issuers.

insights.claim: Jacobs' personal framework for filtering market noise is to ignore daily news and product upgrades and anchor only on identifiable inflection points - a major technology breakthrough, a major regulatory change, or a major societal shift - built on top of a low-cost, tax-efficient, liquid core portfolio.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A usable filter for deciding when a headline deserves a portfolio change versus when it is noise, especially in fast-moving AI and crypto news cycles.
insights.quote: It's not about the news on a day-to-day basis. It's not about some rumor or some company with necessarily just kind of a new product upgrade. What's changed?

insights.claim: Jacobs identifies ChatGPT's November 2022 launch as the AI inflection point precisely because the underlying model was already a couple of years old and not especially new - the chat interface, not the model, unlocked mass participation and the fastest-growing online platform ever.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Inflection points come from access and interface changes rather than raw capability - the same logic Jacobs applies to IBIT and Bitcoin, and a template for spotting the next one.
insights.quote: It was a couple years old already, but they introduced a chat box which meant that so many more people to could participate in it

insights.claim: BlackRock's public thematic midyear update at iShares.com/insights focuses on the next phase of AI, the choke points in the buildout, and opportunities in sectors outside technology, rather than on the current state of AI.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A directly checkable primary source for the bottleneck thesis described in this conversation.

themes.theme: Generational wealth transfer and self-directed channel

insights.claim: The self-directed and independent investor channel is one of the fastest-growing client channels, but BlackRock finds end investors range from high-conviction traders wanting laser-specific exposures to first-time savers with $100 wanting something resembling a 401k - requiring different products and different education, not just different marketing.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: The retail channel is bifurcating rather than homogenizing, which supports both hyper-specific tactical products and low-cost core products at the expense of the middle.

insights.claim: Jacobs argues IBIT's success is partly explained by advisers recognizing they cannot use the same product conversation with baby boomer clients and millennial clients, and needing to be conversant in Bitcoin to bridge the generations through the coming wealth transfer.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: Adviser client-retention pressure, not adviser conviction in Bitcoin, may be the underappreciated driver of continued IBIT flows during the wealth transfer.
insights.quote: the parents saying, you know, talk to me about your large cap growth fund and the kid is saying, tell me about your Bitcoin fund

insights.claim: Data from the host's consumer platform Sylvia shows its users - a crypto-leaning audience - hold roughly 20% of assets in primary residence or real estate, only about 10% in crypto, and the bulk in public equities, contradicting the narrative that younger fintech users are overwhelmingly crypto-allocated.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Even in the most crypto-sympathetic retail cohort, allocation sits near 10% - a sober anchor for sizing the realistic ceiling on retail crypto flows versus the headline narrative.
insights.quote: Only 10% is crypto.

insights.claim: Jacobs holds that the fundamental principles of portfolio construction are not generational - only the instruments, structures and asset classes evolve - so the adviser's job in the wealth transfer is behavioral coaching toward end goals rather than reinventing method.
insights.speaker: Jay Jacobs
insights.so_what: A counterweight to the view that generational preference shifts will restructure asset allocation wholesale; expect vehicle migration more than risk-return regime change.
insights.quote: the fundamental principles of portfolio management don't change
